title: Static abstract members and generic math
body: Interfaces can declare `static abstract` members (C# 11), which implementing types must provide as static members. Generic code constrained to such an interface can call them through the type parameter: `T.Zero`, `T.Parse(text, null)`, or operators like `a + b`. This makes 'factory' and 'operator' contracts possible without instances.

.NET uses this for generic math. `INumber<T>` and its smaller pieces (`IAdditionOperators<TSelf, TOther, TResult>`, `IAdditiveIdentity<TSelf, TResult>`, `IComparisonOperators`, `IParsable<TSelf>`) are implemented by all built-in numeric types. One `Sum<T>(IEnumerable<T>) where T : INumber<T>` works for int, double, decimal and BigInteger.

Your own types can participate: a `Money` or `Vector` struct implementing `IAdditionOperators<Money, Money, Money>` and `IAdditiveIdentity<Money, Money>` works with any algorithm written against those interfaces. Constrain to the smallest interface the algorithm needs.

The `TSelf` pattern (`where TSelf : IThing<TSelf>`) lets the interface refer to the implementing type. Static virtual members (with a default body) are also allowed. C# 15 adds non-virtual static interface members, covered in the final stage.

Generic math code is compiled per value type, so it runs as fast as hand-written code. Check overflow behaviour: `T.CreateChecked(x)` throws when a value does not fit, `CreateSaturating` clamps and `CreateTruncating` wraps.

challenge: Write a generic Max<T>(ReadOnlySpan<T> values) where T : INumber<T> that throws for an empty span, and call it with int and double arrays.
question: What lets generic code write `T.AdditiveIdentity` or `a + b` for a type parameter T?
correct: Constraining T to interfaces with static abstract members
reasoning: Static abstract interface members expose operators and static factories to generic code at compile time.
